title: Why Your ADC Sees Signals That Aren’t There.  #electronics
description:
High-frequency noise at an ADC input can show up in your microcontroller data as a clean, slow, low-frequency waveform. That is the danger of aliasing: the error does not look like random noise. It looks like a real signal.

In this video, we break down how ADC aliasing works using a simple example: a 101 Hz sine wave sampled at 100 samples per second. The result is a sampled sequence that looks like a 1 Hz ghost signal.

This is not a random firmware bug or a bad sensor. It is a direct consequence of sampling. Once a high-frequency component is sampled incorrectly, it can fold down into the digital data as a false low-frequency component.

We also look at a practical measurement example: a temperature sensor near a switching power supply. Even if the real sensor value is stable, high-frequency ripple can couple into the ADC input through the power rail, ground return, a long cable, or poor PCB layout. If that noise is present before sampling, it can become a slow drift in the data.

The key takeaway: anti-aliasing must happen before the ADC. A digital filter after sampling cannot remove an alias that already looks like a real low-frequency signal.

Topics covered:

ADC sampling and aliasing
Why 101 Hz can look like 1 Hz
Spectral folding
The Nyquist condition
High-frequency noise in real measurements
Why anti-aliasing filters go before the ADC
RC filters for ADC inputs

title: Designing an Ultra-Pure Delta-Sigma Generator on FPGA | Part 2
description:
Ever spent hours debugging a digital filter only to realize the 'perfect' sine wave from your bench signal generator is actually full of unexpected spurs? You're not alone.

In this video, we attack the problem directly. Instead of buying a high-end precision source worth thousands of dollars, we are building our own ultra-pure signal generator using an affordable Cyclone IV FPGA. To properly test modern 12-bit ADCs without our equipment becoming the bottleneck, we need a massive 98 dBFS of dynamic range.

We dig into the implementation details of a second-order Delta-Sigma (DS) modulator, explaining how aggressive noise shaping pushes quantization noise out of our target band. Before we touch the real FPGA fabric, we build a complete software simulation of the classic Boser-Wooley architecture. The result? A solid 113.8 dB of theoretical margin.

But the real fight for decibels is just beginning. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2, where we write the RTL code and battle hardware realities like clock jitter, phase truncation, and power supply noise!

title: PWM vs. Sigma-Delta for 1-Pin DACs: Tradeoffs and Limits. #PWM #PDM
description:
Have you ever wondered why increasing the timer clock on a microcontroller doesn't automatically yield a clean, high-resolution PWM output? On paper, the math is simple. In practice, you hit a hard tradeoff between bit resolution and sampling frequency.

Today, we dive deep into the engineering challenge of building a 1-bit DAC using a single digital pin and a simple output filter. We compare two fundamental approaches: Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) and Sigma-Delta (ΣΔ) modulation.

In this episode, we run dedicated testbench simulations to analyze the spectral energy distribution of both architectures. You will learn:

The Math Behind PWM Limits: Why high-resolution PWM inevitably pushes the carrier frequency down, complicating output filtering.

Quantization Noise Shaping: How Sigma-Delta modulators push noise out of band and shift it to higher frequencies, resulting in relaxed filter requirements.

Practical Trade-offs: Why PWM offers low signal-path latency and easier switching-loss estimation (crucial for motor drives, DC-DC converters, LED drivers, and power stages), while ΣΔ is well suited for audio and simple test signals.

Hardware Realities: A look into how modern MCUs (STM32, ESP32) implement these concepts at the silicon level.

Ultimately, there is no universal one-pin DAC. The right choice depends entirely on your system's requirements for spectral purity, loop delay, and stability.

01:02 — Goal: Building a DAC using a single digital pin.

title: Why Your MOSFET Keeps Burning Out (The Hidden Transistor) #electronics
description:

In this video, we uncover the hidden anatomy of a power N-channel MOSFET and explain how high dV/dt or avalanche operation can trigger the deadly "latch-up" effect. Once it turns on, you lose gate control, and the component dies in milliseconds.

title: Why Your MOSFETs Keep Failing (And How to Actually Read the Datasheet)
description:
Ideally, a power MOSFET would behave like an ideal switch. In reality, it is a highly nonlinear semiconductor device filled with parasitic effects, hidden tradeoffs, and failure mechanisms.

In this episode of High SNR, we go inside the silicon die to examine the “ghosts” living inside a power transistor and explain what the datasheet is really telling you.

Using a vertical N-channel power MOSFET as the example device, we cover four critical aspects of real-world MOSFET behavior:

🔹 Die topology and on-resistance — the tradeoff among RDS(on), parasitic JFET resistance, and input capacitance (Ciss)
🔹 Body diode dynamics — why reverse-recovery charge (Qrr) and snap-off effects create hard-switching problems and EMI
🔹 The parasitic bipolar transistor — how high dV/dt and avalanche conditions can trigger destructive latch-up
🔹 The Miller plateau — why switching losses are tightly linked to charging the reverse-transfer capacitance while the device operates in the linear region

From the early history of Fairchild Semiconductor and sodium-ion contamination to the practical limits of modern planar MOSFET geometry, this episode breaks down the device physics behind one of the most important components in power electronics.

Note: This episode focuses on a vertical N-channel power MOSFET, using the FQP19N20C as a reference device. Here, planar refers specifically to the gate structure in which the inversion channel forms laterally at the die surface.

title: Stop Oversizing MOSFETs: The Hidden Thermal Cost of Voltage Margins
description:
Blindly doubling your MOSFET voltage rating to handle transients isn't "playing it safe" - it's an engineering mistake that destroys converter efficiency. 

In this episode, we debunk the "Just-in-case" margin myth. We dive deep into the silicon physics to explain why higher breakdown voltages exponentially increase RDS(on) and thermal losses. You'll learn how different engineering domains  - from heavy industrial motor drives to compact DC-DC telecom converters, and even NASA deep-space probes like Voyager 1 - calculate their voltage derating factors.

Stop treating symptoms with oversized silicon. Learn how to attack the root causes of inductive voltage spikes.

title: Stable Transistor Design: Collector-to-Base Feedback Explained.  #electronics
description:
Why does a clean sine wave suddenly drift and distort? In this video, we analyze the impact of temperature on Bipolar Junction Transistors (BJT) and explore a simple yet elegant solution to prevent thermal runaway.

We break down the logic of Collector-to-Base feedback—a negative voltage feedback method that uses only two resistors to keep the operating point stable. You will learn:

- Why collector current doubles with a 10°C temperature rise.
- How to implement stabilization without overcomplicating the circuit.
- The trade-offs between gain, stability, and the Miller effect.
- Perfect for electronics engineers and hobbyists looking to build more reliable hardware.

title: Why Cold Kills MOSFETs Faster Than Heat #electronics
description:
Most engineers are obsessed with cooling: heat sinks, fans, and thermal paste are everywhere. But there is a silent killer that can destroy your MOSFET much faster than overheating — extreme cold. 
In this video, we dive into the V_(BR)DSS parameter (Drain-to-Source Breakdown Voltage) and reveal why a drop in temperature can lead to a catastrophic avalanche breakdown. 
We’ll look at a real-world datasheet example to see how a "safe" 100V rating at room temperature can shrink to a dangerous 93V in freezing conditions.
What you will learn:
Why silicon MOSFETs have a positive temperature coefficient.
How to read the breakdown voltage charts correctly.
Why your outdoor electronics might be failing despite perfect thermal management.
The golden rule of designing with a "cold margin."
If you are designing devices for harsh environments or outdoor use, this technical deep dive is a must-watch. Don't let the frost vaporize your hard work!

title: Why Your MOSFETs Keep Blowing Up (Datasheet Secrets Revealed)
description:
We manufacture insulated-gate field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) in quantities far exceeding the total number of stars in the known universe. Yet, despite producing them by the trillions, many engineers still misread their datasheets, leading to catastrophic circuit failures.

Welcome to the High SNR channel! In this video, we dive deep into the fine print of power MOSFET specifications. We are investigating the drain-to-source breakdown voltage (VDSS) - a parameter that seems like an absolute constant right up until it starts drifting due to temperature drops or inductive spikes.

If you usually skip the introductory text and scroll straight to the tables, this video is for you. We’ll uncover the myth of breakdown voltage, explain the fatal errors engineers make with single-pulse avalanche energy (EAS), and show you why crossing the right-hand boundary of the Safe Operating Area (SOA) is a strict law of physics.

Always design your circuits with a solid safety margin, and never forget to read the fine print!

title: Why Your MOSFET Failed: The Truth About Eas  Ratings #electronics
description:
Many engineers assume that if a drain voltage spike exceeds the V_DSS rating, it's instant death for the transistor. Not necessarily. Modern MOSFETs are designed to handle brief overvoltage events in avalanche mode.

In this video, we break down a critical datasheet parameter: Single Pulse Avalanche Energy E_AS. You will learn why that impressive energy figure typically found on the first page of a datasheet can be highly misleading.

We reveal the main "catch": The allowable avalanche energy drops dramatically as the junction temperature T_J rises. A design that is safe on a cold bench at 25°C can easily fail at operating temperatures of 100°C or more. Don't ignore the thermal derating curve!
